Laura Luebbert 1,2,3,4 , Delaney K. Sullivan1,2,5, Maria Carilli1,2, Kristján Eldjárn Hjörleifsson1,2, Alexander Viloria Winnett1,5, Tara Chari 1,2,3 & Lior Pachter 1,2

The increasing use of high-throughput sequencing methods in research, agriculture and healthcare provides an opportunity for the cost-effective surveillance of viral diversity and investigation of virus–disease correlation. However, existing methods for identifying viruses in sequencing data rely on and are limited to reference genomes or cannot retain single-cell resolution through cell barcode tracking. We introduce a method that accurately and rapidly detects viral sequences in bulk and single-cell transcriptomics data based on the highly conserved RdRP protein, enabling the detection of over 100,000 RNA virus species. The analysis of viral presence and host gene expression in parallel at single-cell resolution allows for the characterization of host viromes and the identification of viral tropism and host responses. We apply our method to peripheral blood mononuclear cell data from rhesus macaques with Ebola virus disease and describe previously unknown putative viruses. Moreover, we are able to accurately predict viral presence in individual cells based on macaque gene expression.

There are an estimated 300,000 mammalian viruses1 from which infectious diseases in humans may arise2, although only a fraction can currently be detected. For example, in a recent study, only 261 virus species were directly detected in humans by using PCR or sequencing3. Detectable viruses have been implicated in heart disease and cancer4,5, as well as neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and multiple sclerosis6–8. Accurate detection of viruses is crucial to identifying viral contributions to human health and disease. Of the 261 known disease-causing viruses, 206 fall into the realm of Riboviria3, which includes RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP)-encoding RNA viruses and RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (RdDP)-encoding retroviruses. These include corona, dengue, Ebola, hepatitis B, influenza, measles, mumps, polio, West Nile and Zika viruses. Most existing workflows for detecting viruses

in transcriptomics data rely on pre-assembled reference genomes. As of November 2024, National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) RefSeq hosts 8,694 Riboviria reference genomes—a diminutive fraction of Riboviria viruses9. Recent pioneering work10 leveraged a well-conserved amino acid sub-sequence of the RdRP, called the ‘palmprint’, to identify RNA viruses in 5.7 million globally and ecologically diverse sequencing samples from the Sequence Read Archive. The independence of their method from pre-computed indices enabled the discovery of thousands of viruses and resulted in a consensus of 296,623 unique RdRP-containing amino acid sequences, hereafter referred to as the ‘PalmDB’. Clustering palmprints into species-like operational taxonomic units (sOTUs) yielded 146,973 sOTUs10,11, which enables the detection of 16× more viruses than the 8,694 Riboviria reference genomes currently available on NCBI. We then tested whether our translated search method is robust to single nucleotide mutations, which occur at a relatively high rate in RNA viruses41. We added random single nucleotide base substitutions to 676 EBOV nucleotide RdRP sequences and then assessed the frequency of correct taxonomic classification (recall percentage) by kallisto translated search and compared it to standard nucleotide alignment with kallisto and the current state-of-the-art translated search tool, Kraken2 (translated search). Kallisto translated search correctly recalled up to 27.5% more viral RdRP sequences than Kraken2

Read and virus filtering Cross-species contamination of reference genome databases42–44 can lead to the misclassification of host reads as bacterial or viral, hindering correct identification of microbial or viral sequences. This misclassification can be prevented by removing host reads before the alignment to the viral reference. However, removal of host reads results in the removal of sequences from endogenous viral elements abundant in vertebrate genomes45 and may inadvertently remove viral sequences that were truly present. Hence, there are two goals: removing host reads to prevent the misclassification of host reads as viral while comprehensively identifying the virome within a sample. We developed a series of sequence-masking options to identify reads that align to both host and virus or microbe while preserving all reads (virus only and host or virus ambiguous) for downstream

analysis (Fig. 3a,b, Extended Data Fig. 3b and Supplementary Note). These methods can be applied to mask any nucleotide or amino acid reference. We first evaluated the impact of different host-masking options on the resulting virome. Using kallisto translated search with the PalmDB, we mapped the virus profiles of PBMC RNA-seq samples from 19 rhesus macaques39. To confirm that reads identified as viral were not misaligned macaque reads, we extracted a subset of sequencing reads from 11 virus IDs and aligned them against the nucleotide sequence database with BLAST+46,47 (Extended Data Fig. 5a). Given that the majority of RdRP sequences in the PalmDB originate from unknown viruses lacking reference genomes, it was expected that these sequences would not produce confident BLAST matches, whereas misaligned macaque reads should match the well-defined macaque genome48 with high coverage and identity. Virus-like sequences not removed by any masking option aligned non-specifically to several superkingdoms, including viruses, but not with high coverage or identity to macaque.

The specifics of host versus viral read masking and the approach to handling reference sequences affect the resulting virome (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Figs. 3b, 5b and 6). Depending on the research question and study design, any one or a combination of different masking options might be appropriate (Fig. 3a, Extended Data Fig. 5b and Supplementary Note). In some instances, conservative masking with BWA software (‘prior alignment to host’) seemed to have removed probable viral sequences (u11150; further evidence provided below), whereas in another instance (u41991), it retained sequences that BLAST-aligned to the macaque genome that were masked by the kallisto D-list + host capture workflow (Supplementary Note). Separately from exploring the results of different read-masking options, we also investigated the question of virus filtering. Host read capture with kallisto generates two separate count matrices: one contains counts for reads that are solely viral and a second contains counts for viral reads that also pseudoalign to the host transcriptome. The important distinction between filtering reads and filtering viruses becomes evident when examining the two count matrices. For the macaque PBMC dataset, we found that most viruses found in ≥0.05% of cells, including the confirmed virus EBOV, had at least some reads

that also mapped to the host transcriptome (Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 5b). Hence, naive masking of reads can lower the detection sensitivity of viruses. Our masking workflows thus facilitate the identification of viruses while also identifying certain unmasked reads that may correspond to viruses, to prevent the decrease in sensitivity inherent in masking host reads. We applied this approach when training the logistic regression models described below to minimize false negatives when detecting viruses at single-cell resolution.

We first sought to determine the virus-like sequences that might have been introduced through reagent or sample contamination. To do so, we reasoned that viruses occurring in both macaque samples and in a subset of samples that included a spike-in of Madin–Darby canine kidney (MDCK) cells (Extended Data Fig. 7b,c) would probably represent laboratory contaminants51. We compared virus IDs found in ‘macaque only’, ‘MDCK only’ or ‘shared’ (Fig. 4b). We detected four virus IDs (including EBOV) present only in macaque, seven in MDCK, 54 shared and 15 undefined virus IDs. Furthermore, many virus IDs in the shared category were also detected in ‘blank’ sequencing libraries of only sterile water and reagent mix, supporting that they originated from laboratory reagent contamination51 (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 8a). Next, we explored the virus taxa that were observed in the data. The sOTUs of the macaque-only and shared virus IDs, when available, are listed in Supplementary Table 1. Figure 4c shows the fraction of reads occupied by each viral order for macaque-only, MDCK-only and shared viruses. Among viruses shared between macaque and MDCK cells, Norzivirales (formerly Levivirales), Articulavirales (which include the family of influenza viruses) and viruses of unknown taxonomy made up the largest fractions. Norzivirales are an order of bacteriophages, the majority of which were discovered in metagenomics studies52. They might have been introduced through bacterial contamination during sample preparation and sequencing. The shared viruses also included orders such as Herpesvirales, which are widespread, including across species, and are known to persist in hosts as latent infection53,54. Virus-like sequences detected in MDCK cells included sOTUs from the order of Elliovirales (formerly Bunyavirales), which infect a wide range of hosts, including MDCK cells55, as well as virus-like sequences of unknown order. Virus-like sequences found only in macaque cells were of the order Mononegavirales, which includes EBOV, the order Nidovirales, which are known to infect mammals and include the family Coronaviridae, and an unknown order. Overall, virus-like sequences of known order for each group are reasonably expected to be present in the respective hosts, which supports the biological validity of these viral read classifications. To visualize the viromes of individual animals over time, we plotted viral abundance (the fraction of positive cells) for each virus ID per animal and time point (Fig. 4d). The viral abundances varied, both between individual monkeys and time points, though longitudinal samples from the same animal showed consistency over time (Figs. 4d and 6a). For example, the viromes of animal NHP08 at −4 days and 6 days post infection with EBOV are highlighted in the heatmap (Fig. 4d). NHP1 and NHP2 each had two samples sequenced 20 h apart, which displayed highly similar viromes for each animal over time (Fig. 6a). This stability of the virome within an animal over time is consistent with expectation. Next, we attempted to determine which virus-like sequences were probably present as a result of viral infection of the host. Excluding EBOV, two of three virus IDs found only in macaque samples exhibited cell type specificity suggestive of infection: u102540 (Alphacoronavirus sp.) and u11150 (Fig. 5c). u102540 and u11150 were highly abundant among neutrophils and less abundant in monocytes, B cells and T cells. This difference may be caused by viral tropism for neutrophils or the phagocytic nature of neutrophils engulfing virions or viral RNA. The third virus ID found only in macaque samples, u39566, was expressed more evenly across all cell types and samples, similar to the shared viruses u134800 and u102324 (Fig. 5c, Extended Data Fig. 8b and Supplementary Table 1). u39566 was also identified in the blank sequencing libraries (Extended Data Fig. 8a), further suggesting contamination rather than infection.

Given that our workflow operates at single-cell resolution, we could study viral presence along with host gene expression within a cell. An association between the presence of virus and perturbed host gene expression would support that the virus is causing infection or being actively cleared. We trained logistic regression models for all macaque-only and shared virus IDs to predict viral presence or absence in individual cells based on the cell’s host gene expression. We found that the presence of viruses probably related to infection (u10 (EBOV), u102540 and u11150) could be predicted at >70% accuracy based on host gene expression (Fig. 6b,c). However, for u11150, the sensitivity decreased with the inclusion of the covariates donor animal and EVD time point (Extended Data Fig. 9a). By contrast, the presence of viruses that did not display cell type specificity indicative of infection (u39566, u134800 and u102324) could not be predicted better than random chance (50%) (Fig. 6b,c and Extended Data Fig. 9a). This relationship between viral presence and host gene expression provides further evidence that reads from u10, the known infection with EBOV, as well as novel virus-like sequences u102540 and potentially u11150, were caused by viral infection and/or viral clearance. Lastly, we reasoned that host genes predictive of viral presence would be within known cellular signalling pathways related to viral clearance or immune responses. We identified macaque genes with the largest predictive power and smallest variation across the regression models described above, initialized with different random seeds (Extended Data Fig. 10a). The most highly and consistently weighted genes for u10 (EBOV) were significantly enriched for several virus-associated Gene Ontology (GO) terms, including ‘Negative regulation of viral entry into host cell (GO:0046597)’, ‘Negative regulation of viral life cycle (GO:1903901)’ and ‘Regulation of viral entry into host cell (GO:0046596)’ (Extended Data Fig. 10b). Although the adjusted enrichment P values for the novel virus IDs u11150 and u102540 were not significant, the highly weighted genes for u11150 included CTSL, which is involved in ‘Antigen processing and presentation of peptide antigen via MHC Class II (GO:0002495)’ and ‘Receptor-mediated endocytosis of virus by host cell (GO:0019065)’. For virus ID u102540, several GO terms were indicative of an inflammatory response, such as ‘Positive regulation of type II interferon production (GO:0032729)’ and ‘Positive regulation of cytokine production (GO:0001819)’. Several predictive genes were associated with the positive regulation of cytokine production and modulation of inflammation (for example, FCN1 for u10, MAPK11 for u11150 and CD14 for u102540). Overall, these results provide further evidence that the presence of novel virus-like sequences u102540 and u11150 correlates with a host gene response.

Discussion Our work provides a method for extracting a ‘virome’ modality from any bulk or single-cell RNA-seq data by leveraging a method that maps and quantifies species-level viral RdRP sequences using an amino acid sequence reference. We built on the existing alignment software kallisto30,31 and bustools56 and expanded them for translated alignment by (reverse) translating both the amino acid reference and the nucleotide sequencing reads into a common, non-redundant, comma-free code. Although we validated kallisto translated search in combination with the PalmDB for identification of viral RNA, our workflow can be applied in combination with any amino acid reference, including other databases of RdRP sequences29,57,58. For example, amino acid sequences of antimicrobial peptides59 can be used as a reference to identify these peptides in bulk and single-cell RNA-seq data. Moreover, amino acid transcriptomes of homologous species may be used as a reference for species with missing or incomplete reference genomes for which pseudoalignment in the amino acid space will decrease sensitivity to single nucleotide mutations. We validated kallisto translated search in combination with the PalmDB for detection and identification of viral RNA in next-generation sequencing data at single-cell resolution. We have shown that such monitoring and virus discovery could be performed using single-cell RNA-seq data. Moreover, our work provides a platform for characterizing omnipresent virus-like sequences associated with different environments, hosts and laboratory reagents. Despite the versatility of our approach, it is important to acknowledge its limitations, such as the sparsity of the generated virus count matrix as well as challenges in correctly masking host sequences and interpreting virus-like sequences (further described in the Supplementary Discussion). Our workflow is best used in combination with complementary tools such as BLAST46, Kraken2 (ref. 28) and/or nucleotide alignment to the reference genome when available to improve confidence in viral detection. The strength of our tool lies in its ability to provide a rapid and comprehensive overview of the virus-like sequences present in a sample, enabling targeted downstream analyses. Finally, in optimizing kallisto translated search, we have identified several experimental design choices that greatly impact the results of viral and microbial read quantification, such as sample spike-ins, blank reagent controls and sequencing primer design (Supplementary Discussion). The masking workflows described in this paper and the associated challenges are applicable to any metagenomics analysis in addition to the identification of viral reads, and the workflows described here can be easily applied to nucleotide references, such as a 16S database for the characterization of the human gut microbiome60.

Methods Developing kallisto translated search and optimization for the identification of viral RNA Building kallisto translated search and choosing a new ‘genetic code’. To perform translated alignment, the nucleotide and amino acid sequences need to be translated into a shared ‘language’. This could potentially be achieved by translating nucleotides to amino acids or vice versa. Given that kallisto encodes nucleotide characters in two bits (allowing a total of four distinct nucleotides to be encoded), encoding the 20 different amino acids resulting from translated nucleotide sequences was not feasible. Moreover, reverse-translating the amino acid sequences to nucleotides would be intractable because of the redundancy in the genetic code leading to a combinatorial explosion in nucleotide sequences. Therefore, we translated the nucleotide sequences and reverse-translated the amino acid sequences using a fixed synthetic code designed to reduce spurious alignments. We explored two different codes for this translation: comma-free code and a code that maximizes the Hamming distance between frequently occurring amino acids (Extended Data Fig. 2a). Although maximizing Hamming distance is advantageous in terms of avoiding sequence multimapping (see next paragraph), a comma-free code, further described in the next paragraph, prevents off-frame alignment because any k-mers formed by adjacent words will not be included in the dictionary. We found that the comma-free code recalls viral sequences equally well compared to maximizing the Hamming distance between amino acids (Extended Data Fig. 2b). The translated alignment is performed by first reverse-translating the amino acid reference sequences and all possible reading frames (three forward and three reverse) of the nucleotide sequencing reads to comma-free code (Supplementary Fig. 1)64. A comma-free code is a set of k-letter ‘words’ selected such that any off-frame k-mers formed by adjacent letters do not constitute a ‘word’, and will thus be interpreted as ‘nonsense’. For k = 3 (a triplet code) and four letters (for example, ‘A’, ‘T’, ‘C’ and ‘G’), this results in exactly 20 possible words (theorem shown in Supplementary Fig. 1), which equals the number of amino acids specified by the universal genetic code. The De Bruijn graph generated from the reverse-translated PalmDB sequences groups viruses of the same taxonomies, indicating that within-taxonomy similarity is conserved in comma-free space, as expected (Extended Data Fig. 3a). Finally, the six reading frames of the sequencing reads translated to comma-free code are pseudoaligned to the reference sequences reverse-translated to comma-free code. If several reading frames of the same read produce alignments, the best frame is chosen (Supplementary Fig. 1).

Optimization of PalmDB for the identification of viral reads in RNA-seq data. Owing to the high similarity between viral RdRP sequences, the loss of aligned sequences caused by multimapping to several reference sequences was a major concern. Moreover, the necessity of reverse-translating the amino acid sequences further decreases the Hamming distance between reference sequences by approximately 30% (Extended Data Fig. 2d). To overcome this problem, we tried clustering the amino acid sequences based on 99% similarity using MMseqs2 (release 15-6f452)65. This resulted in 6,518 clusters with high concordance of taxonomy labels between sequences in the same cluster (Extended Data Fig. 2e). However, although clusters were computed correctly based on their concordance with taxonomy, this resulted in 67.4% of sOTUs not being detected anymore (compared to 3.3% when using the complete index). As a result, we decided to group the sOTUs instead, treating virus IDs with the same taxonomy across all main taxonomic ranks like transcripts of the same gene (available at https://tinyurl.com/4wd33rey). This retained the alignment percentage of the complete index while allowing highly accurate taxonomic assignment and minimal sequence loss to multimapping (Fig. 2b). It is noteworthy that the default kallisto k-mer length of 31 nucleotides equals only ten amino acids. Given the architecture of the current

kallisto version (0.50.1), which is optimized for 64-bit k-mers with each nucleotide occupying two bits, k cannot be set to >31. This will change in future versions of kallisto.

Validation and benchmarks Visualization of the Kraken2 and kallisto translated search alignments of EBOV sequences. Kotliar et al.39 performed single-cell RNA-seq of PBMC samples from rhesus macaques after infection with EBOV (further described below). A subset of the data obtained by these authors at 8 days post infection with EBOV was used to visualize the identification of RdRP sequences using kallisto (v.0.50.0) translated search. The first 100,000,000 raw sequencing reads from the GSE158390 library SRR12698539 were aligned to the EBOV reference genome (NC_002549.1) using Kraken2 (v.2.1.2) and to the optimized PalmDB using kallisto translated search. Testing robustness to mutation. Mutation-Simulator63 (v.3.0.1) was used to add random single nucleotide base substitutions to 676 O. zairense (EBOV) RdRP sequences identified as described in the previous paragraph at increasing mutation rates. We performed ten rounds of simulated mutations per mutation rate. The sequences were subsequently aligned using kallisto translated search against the complete PalmDB, DIAMOND70 translated search against the RdRP amino acid sequence of EBOV, Kraken2 translated search against the RdRP amino acid sequence of EBOV with a manually adjusted NCBI Taxonomy ID to allow compatibility with Kraken2, and kallisto standard workflow against the complete EBOV nucleotide genome (GCA_000848505.1). The DIAMOND translated alignment was performed using the gget diamond71 module (gget v.0.29.1). We subsequently calculated the recall percentage over all 676 sequences for kallisto and Kraken2 (Fig. 1c) and the average identity percentage and number of sequences aligned for DIAMOND (Extended Data Fig. 3c). For kallisto translated search, the recall percentage was calculated based on species-level taxonomic assignment. As the other two methods were only given the target virus sequence as a reference and did not have to distinguish between different viruses, their recall percentage was calculated based on all aligned sequences. The recall percentage over all 676 sequences for the ten rounds at each mutation rate is shown in Fig. 1c. Extended Data Fig. 3d shows the precision with which kallisto translated search identified the correct virus versus other taxonomies at each mutation rate. The recall and precision at mutation rates of >0 were fitted with an inverse sigmoid function using non-linear least squares and the scipy.optimize. curve_fit function (scipy v.1.11.1).

The sequencing reads for each library used in the validation (Fig. 2a) were aligned with kallisto translated search against the PalmDB index D-listed with the corresponding host genome and transcriptome. The hosts were human (GRCh38 Ensembl version 109) for GSE150316, GSM4548303 and the SARS-CoV-2 saliva, nasal and throat samples; mouse (GRCm39 Ensembl version 109) for GSM5974202; and rhesus macaque (Mmul_10 Ensembl version 109) and dog (ROS_Cfam_1.0 Ensembl version 109) for GSE158390. Analysis of macaque PBMC data Kotliar et al.39 performed single-cell RNA-seq of PBMC samples from 19 rhesus macaques at different time points during EVD after infection with EBOV (EBOV/Kikwit; GenBank accession MG572235.1; Filoviridae: Zaire ebolavirus (renamed to Orthoebolavirus zairense)) using Seq-Well35 with the S3 protocol74. A subset of PBMC samples were spiked with MDCK cells. The data are available at GSE158390, and we obtained the raw sequencing data from the European Nucleotide Archive using FTP download links and ffq (v.0.3.0)75. The data are split into 106 datasets containing 30,594,130,037 reads in total.

Alignment to the host transcriptome. The rhesus macaque Mmul_10 and domestic dog ROS_Cfam_1.0 genomes were retrieved from Ensembl (v.109). The reference index was built using both genomes and the kb-python (v.0.28.0 with kallisto v.0.50.0 and bustools v.0.43.1) ref command to create a combined index containing the transcriptome of both species. We quantified the gene expression in each of the 106 datasets using the standard kallisto-bustools workflow30 with the ‘batch’ and ‘batch-barcodes’ arguments to process all files simultaneously while keeping track of each batch, and with the ‘x’-string ‘0,0,12:0,12,20:1,0,0’ to match the Seq-Well technology. Given that the Seq-Well technology does not provide a barcode on-list, we generated a barcode on-list using the ‘bustools allowlist’ command, requiring each barcode to occur at least 1,000 times. We subsequently corrected the cell barcodes using the generated on-list and computed the count matrix using the ‘bustools count’ function.

Host cell quality control, filtering and separation of macaque and MDCK cells. The count matrix generated by bustools was converted to h5ad using kb_python.utils.kb_utils and read into Python using anndata (v.0.8.0). Metadata such as donor animal, the presence of an MDCK spike-in and time point were added to the AnnData object from the SRR library metadata provided by Kotliar et al.39. The cell barcodes were filtered based on a minimum number of unique molecular identifier (UMI) counts of 125 obtained from the knee plot of sorted total UMI counts per cell (Extended Data Fig. 7a), resulting in a mean UMI count of 1,401 after filtering. The cells were further filtered based on a maximum percentage of mitochondrial genes of 10%, based on a combination of macaque and dog mitochondrial genes facilitated by Scanpy76 (v.1.9.3) and gget71 (v.0.28.0). Cells were categorized as macaque if a maximum of 10% of their UMIs originated from dog genes and vice versa (Extended Data Fig. 7b). Macaque and MDCK cells were normalized separately using log(CP10k + 1) with Scanpy’s normalize_total defaults of target sum 10,000 and log1p.

Macaque cell clustering and cell type assignment. The macaque gene count matrix was transformed by PCA to 50 dimensions, applied

using the log-normalized counts filtered for highly variable genes using Scanpy’s highly_variable_genes. Next, we computed nearest neighbours and conducted Leiden clustering49 using Scanpy, resulting in 19 Leiden clusters. We found that EVD time points were highly concordant across sequencing libraries, suggesting the lack of a batch effect (Fig. 5a; also see GitHub code repository). Each cluster was manually annotated with a cell type based on the expression of previously established marker genes39 (Extended Data Fig. 7d). Cluster ‘undefined 1’ was omitted because it only contained 12 cells. Gene names and descriptions for Ensembl IDs without annotations were obtained using gget71. The obtained cell types, their marker gene expression and relative abundance over time are consistent with the results reported in the Kotliar et al. publication39, including the emergence of a cluster of immature neutrophils and decreased lymphocyte abundance, especially natural killer cells, during EVD (Fig. 5a). Although density-based PBMC isolation typically removes neutrophils, immature neutrophils are less dense than mature neutrophils and can co-isolate with PBMCs during infections39. Clusters of the same cell type were often separated by time point (Fig. 5a), indicating changes in macaque gene expression within the same cell type over the course of the EVD. This is in agreement with results obtained by mass cytometry in Kotliar et al.39.

Virus alignment with different masking options. For each masking option, we quantified the gene expression in each of the 106 datasets from GSE158390 using kallisto with the ‘batch’ and ‘batch-barcodes’ arguments to process all files simultaneously while keeping track of each batch and with the ‘x’-string ‘0,0,12:0,12,20:1,0,0’ to match the Seq-Well technology. kallisto translated search was initiated in the ‘kallisto index’ and ‘kallisto bus’ commands by adding the ‘—aa’ flag. Following the alignment to PalmDB with any of the masking options, cell barcodes were corrected using the barcode on-list generated during the alignment to the host as described above. We explored the following masking workflows, listed from least to most conservative (also see the Supplementary Note).

No mask. The raw sequencing reads were aligned to the optimized PalmDB reference files (see ‘Optimization of PalmDB’ above) using kallisto translated search.

D-list genome + transcriptome. The raw sequencing reads were aligned to the optimized PalmDB reference using kallisto translated search with the added argument ‘d-list’, which was passed the concatenated macaque genome and transcriptome (Mmul_10 Ensembl version 109), and dog genome and transcriptome (ROS_Cfam_1.0 Ensembl version 109). For D-list masking options including only the genomes or transcriptomes (Extended Data Fig. 3b), only the genome or transcriptome files from both species were concatenated and passed to the ‘d-list’ argument, respectively.

D-list genome + transcriptome + ambiguous reads filtered. This workflow was performed as described above for the ‘D-list genome + transcriptome’ with an unreleased version of kallisto (https://tinyurl.com/ mwmy3zwj) in which ambiguous reads in the D-list will be thrown out as host instead of being assigned to virus (Extended Data Fig. 3b). We explored this option to investigate the effect of ambiguous reads during D-list masking. However, we found that the alignment results did not notably differ from the masking option ‘D-list genome + transcriptome’ (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 6).

Host read capture with kallisto. The raw sequencing reads were aligned to the combined macaque and dog reference index generated during the alignment to host with ‘kallisto bus’ with the added ‘-n’ flag. The ‘-n’ flag keeps track of the read line number of each aligned read; the line numbers are added to the resulting BUS file. Prior alignment to host with BWA. The BWA77 (v.0.7.17) ‘bwa index’ command was used to generate a BWA index from the concatenated macaque and dog genomes (Mmul_10 and ROS_Cfam_1.0 from Ensembl v109). For each FASTQ file, the names of all unmapped reads were extracted using ‘samtools view’ (SAMtools67 v.1.6), and a new FASTQ file including only unmapped sequences was generated using the ‘seqtk subseq’ command (v.1.4; https://github.com/lh3/seqtk). The resulting FASTQ files containing the sequencing reads that did not map to the host genomes were aligned to the optimized PalmDB reference files using kallisto translated search.

Extraction and BLAST alignment of viral reads. Randomly selected sequencing reads from three libraries that included reads that mapped to the viruses of interest were aligned to the optimized PalmDB with kallisto translated search including the ‘-n’ flag, without any host read masking. Reads that mapped to the viruses of interest were subsequently captured and extracted from the raw sequencing FASTQ files using ‘bustools capture’ and ‘bustools extract’. The BLAST nt database was downloaded using the BLAST+ (refs. 46,47) (v.2.14.1) update_blastdb.pl command. Ten reads were randomly chosen for each target virus for each SRR library and were BLASTed against the nt database using the blastn algorithm. Sequences that aligned to the polyA tail were recognized by the occurrence of ‘AAAAAAAAAAAA’ or ‘TTTTTTTTTTTT’ in the aligned part of the subject or query sequences and removed from the results. BLAST results were subsequently plotted using pyCirclize.Circos (v.1.0.0; https:// github.com/moshi4/pyCirclize).

Virus quality control and binarization of the virus count matrix. The viral count matrix generated using the ‘Host read capture with kallisto + D-list genome + transcriptome’ masking workflow was converted to h5ad using kb_python.utils.kb_utils and read into Python using anndata. Metadata such as donor animal, the presence of an MDCK spike-in and time point were added to the AnnData object from the SRR library metadata provided by Kotliar et al.39. For each cell, the host species and cell type were added from the host matrices generated as described above. As only a small fraction of the RNA molecules in these tissue samples are viral and, of those, we only detect the RdRP, the measured absolute RNA counts for any one virus per cell are low (Extended Data Fig. 7e). Although we can be confident that cells with at least one virus-like sequence are positive, the counts are generally low at single-cell resolution, and a count of one or two may not reflect a quantitative difference of twofold change. As a result, we converted the virus count matrix into a binary matrix in which each virus was recorded as being either present or not present in each cell. This approach has been previously validated for sparse single-cell RNA; specifically, viral sequencing data24,78. Furthermore, this approach is robust to biases

that may be introduced by normalization methods42,79. The virus IDs were subsequently thresholded to IDs that were observed in ≥0.05% of cells in either species.

Virus categorization into ‘shared’, ‘undefined’, ‘macaque-only’ and ‘MDCK-only’ viruses. For each virus ID, the virus was defined as ‘shared’ if the fold change between the fraction of positive macaque cells and the fraction of positive MDCK cells was ≤2. Viruses were assigned the category ‘macaque only’ if the virus was seen in ≥0.05% of macaque cells and ≤7 MDCK cells, and vice versa for the category ‘MDCK only’. These thresholds were defined based on the percentages of positive cells observed for each virus in each species, as shown in Fig. 4b. Virus IDs falling outside of these thresholds were called ‘undefined’.

Generation of the Krona plot. We generated a data frame containing the total numbers of positive cells for each sOTU seen in ≥0.05% of macaque cells for each animal and time point (including only cells that passed host cell quality control). The KronaTools80 (v.2.8.1) ktImport- Text tool was subsequently used to generate a Krona plot HTML file from a text file generated from this data frame.

Logistic regression models to predict viral presence based on host gene expression. In summary, logistic regression models were either trained on all or only highly variable macaque genes and with or without the donor animal and time point as covariates. Of the top 50 highly variable macaque genes with the largest positive average weights in the regression model, we selected those for which the standard deviation of the weights was less than half of the lowest weight. Here, we used the model trained on highly variable genes with covariates of donor animal and time point. The gene weight distributions and thresholds are shown in Extended Data Fig. 10a. Approximately one-third of the macaque Ensembl IDs did not have annotated gene names. We used gget71 to translate annotated Ensembl IDs to gene symbols and to perform enrichment analysis on the returned gene symbols using Enrichr81 against the 2023 GO Biological Processes database (‘GO_Biological_Process_2023’)82. The background for the enrichment analysis was set to all detected highly variable host genes, which is the full set of genes on which the model used here was trained, with known gene symbols.
